# Deck Review: India Energy Crisis Strategic Intelligence Briefing

---

## 1. TOP 3 CARDS

**Card 1 (c01) — Hero:** Does exactly what an opener should — anchors the "20M bbl/d offline" number against historical precedent with clean comparative bars; instantly establishes severity and earns the reader's next scroll.

**Card 5 (c05) — Strait Reopening Timeline:** The single most strategically valuable card in the deck — reframes the entire crisis from "when does diplomacy work?" to "when do mine sweepers arrive?", which is the actual constraint; changes how the reader thinks.

**Card 11 (c11) — Under-Recovery Waterfall:** Translates a macro crisis into a per-litre P&L reality the board can feel — ₹52/litre loss on every diesel sale is visceral, actionable, and the waterfall visualization makes the cost stack undeniable.

---

## 2. BOTTOM 3 CARDS

**Card 6 (c06) — Act II Break:** Pure filler — "Your refinery" with three preview boxes that say "crude slate disruption / refinery economics / margin compression" tells the reader nothing they won't learn in 3 seconds by scrolling; wastes a full viewport.

**Card 10 (c10) — Act III Break:** Same problem as Card 6 but worse — "three clocks running down" is a metaphor doing the work that data should do; the "next three cards quantify each clock" insight literally admits this card has no content of its own.

**Card 13 (c13) — Brent Outlook:** The headline "Brent is at $100 today. It may not be this low again" is a Goldman Sachs sell-side platitude dressed up as intelligence; the scenario fan chart lacks probability weights and the "3-DIGIT for years" KPI is hand-waving, not analysis.

---

## 3. KILL LIST

- **Card 6 (c06)** — Act II break. Zero incremental information. Delete entirely.
- **Card 10 (c10)** — Act III break. Same. The three-clock framing can be a two-line header on Card 11.
- **Card 2 (c02)** — The $156 peak and rupee data are important but fully redundant with Card 1's stat row and Card 13's Brent chart. Consolidate the USD/INR data point into Card 1 and kill this card.

Removing these three takes the deck from 13+ cards to ~10, which is the maximum a CEO will tolerate.

---

## 4. STORY FLOW — HEADLINE SEQUENCE ANALYSIS

Reading headlines only:

1. *India faces the largest oil supply shock in history* ✅ Strong open
2. *It peaked at $156 per barrel. The rupee hit an all-time low.* ⚠️ Momentum stalls — this is a "what happened" card immediately after a "what happened" card. Two consecutive backward-looking market-impact slides before the reader understands WHY.
3. *22 ships are stranded. Mines make the strait impassable.* ✅ Cause arrives — but should have been Card 2.
4. *Crude is manageable. Cooking gas is rationed for 330M households.* ✅ Good pivot to LPG.
5. *Even a ceasefire cannot reopen the strait until summer.* ✅ Excellent — reframes the timeline.
6. *— Your refinery —* ❌ Dead stop. Momentum dies.
7. *MRPL already shut its crude unit.* ✅ Restarts.
8. *Jamnagar runs at full complexity.* ✅ Good contrast.
9. *The government has overridden your product slate.* ✅ Escalation.
10. *— Your Balance Sheet —* ❌ Another dead stop.
11. *You are losing ₹52 on every litre of diesel.* ✅ Strong.
12. *Russia waiver expires April 3.* ✅ Urgency.
13. *Brent is at $100. It may not be this low again.* ⚠️ Weak close — sounds like a trading recommendation, not a strategic conclusion.

**Where momentum breaks:** Cards 2→3 (effect before cause), Cards 6 and 10 (act breaks that add nothing), and the deck lacks a closing "so what / what to do" card — it just... ends at Card 13 with a price observation.

---

## 5. REDUNDANCY

- **Cards 1 and 2** make the same point: oil prices spiked to historic levels and it's unprecedented. Card 2's $156 peak is the specific instance of Card 1's "largest oil supply shock" claim. Merge.
- **Cards 7 and 8** both argue that single-source refineries are in trouble vs. complex ones. Card 7 is the MRPL case study; Card 8 is the stock performance view of the same thesis. Could be one card with MRPL as the lead example and the stock chart as supporting evidence.
- **Cards 1 and 13** both reference Brent price levels and historical comparison framing. The stat row in Card 1 ("20% global seaborne supply") and Card 13's Brent chart are telling overlapping parts of the same story.

---

## 6. ONE-LINE VERDICT

**No.** This is a 13-card situation report with superb production design but no recommendation architecture — it tells the CEO the building is on fire from seven angles without ever handing them an extinguisher; cut to 9 cards, swap the act breaks for a scenario-probability card and a board-action card, and then it's sendable.

# My Read — 5 Minutes Before Board

---

## 1. TOP 3 CARDS (Clearest Action Items)

**Card 12 — Russia Waiver Expires April 3.**
This is the single most actionable card in the deck. Hard deadline (10 days), clear consequence (secondary sanctions if we process Russian crude post-expiry), and a direct instruction to procurement: find alternative barrels NOW or stop buying Urals. I know what to do and when.

**Card 11 — ₹52/litre Under-Recovery on Diesel.**
This quantifies the bleeding. ₹52 per litre loss on every litre of diesel we sell at frozen retail prices. I can take this number straight to the board and frame the conversation around either seeking government compensation, cutting throughput, or both. The waterfall chart makes the cost build-up undeniable.

**Card 9 — ESMA Override / Product Slate Mandated.**
Government has taken away our optimization lever. Refinery gas cut 35%, LPG prioritized above everything. This tells me my throughput planning team needs to rebuild the production plan around a binding constraint we didn't choose. Actionable immediately.

---

## 2. BOTTOM 3 CARDS (Confused Me or Felt Irrelevant)

**Card 6 — Act II Break ("Your Refinery").**
Pure decoration. Tells me nothing I don't already know. A waste of a scroll in a 23-card deck. Cut it.

**Card 10 — Act III Break ("Your Balance Sheet / Three Clocks").**
Same problem. It's a movie trailer for the next three slides. I don't need a trailer — I need the data. These act breaks feel designed for a presentation audience, not a CFO reading alone before a board meeting.

**Card 1 — Hero Card (20M bbl/d offline, 1970s comparison).**
Visually impressive but strategically useless to me. I already know the Strait is closed. Comparing this to 1973 doesn't help me decide anything. It's context for a journalist, not a CFO. The IEA quote at the bottom is the only useful element, and it could be a single line on the next card.

---

## 3. WHERE I STOPPED READING

**Card 13 — Brent Outlook ("Brent is at $100 today").**

This is where my attention broke. By this point I'd consumed 12 dense cards and was starting to get Goldman Sachs scenario fan charts with "talks succeed / talks fail" paths. The problem: it's speculative where the previous cards were factual. After the precision of the under-recovery math and the sanctions deadline, a "may not be this low again" headline feels like sell-side marketing. I skimmed the rest.

The deck also appears to cut off mid-sentence on Card 13's annotation code — which tells me either the briefing is incomplete or the last 10 cards weren't ready. Either way, I stopped trusting the document here.

---

## 4. MISSING — Questions I Still Have

- **What is our company's specific crude inventory cover in days?** The deck talks about MRPL shutting down and "pipeline cover eroding" but never tells me MY number. Am I at 15 days? 30 days? 45? This is the single most important number for this board meeting and it's absent.
- **What is the total FY26 under-recovery liability estimate?** ₹52/litre is per-unit. What's the aggregate? ₹20,000 crore? ₹40,000 crore? I need the P&L number.
- **Has MoPNG signaled any subsidy reimbursement or retail price revision?** The deck shows the government mandating my product slate but says nothing about whether they'll compensate the margin destruction they're causing.
- **What alternative crude grades are available, at what premium, and with what lead time?** The waiver card tells me to find alternatives but never names them — West African? Guyana? Brazil? At what spread to Brent?
- **Where are the remaining 10 cards?** The deck promised 23 cards. I got ~13 before it cut off. Are the action items and board recommendations in the missing half?

---

## 5. HEADLINE TEST

**Made me scroll immediately:**
- *"You are losing over fifty rupees on every litre of diesel you sell."* — Visceral. Personal. Quantified.
- *"The Russia waiver expires April 3. Your cheapest fallback vanishes in ten days."* — Deadline + consequence in one line.
- *"The government has overridden your product slate. LPG comes first."* — Tells me something changed that affects my operations today.
- *"MRPL already shut its crude unit. Your supply window is closing."* — Peer company action = urgent signal.

**Did NOT make me scroll:**
- *"India faces the largest oil supply shock in history."* — Too broad. I know this.
- *"It peaked at $156 per barrel. The rupee hit an all-time low."* — Past tense. What do I do about it now?
- *"Brent is at $100 today. It may not be this low again."* — Speculative. Feels like a trading desk pitch.
- *"Capacity, slate, and supply are no longer yours to control."* — Dramatic but empty.

---

## 6. ONE-LINE VERDICT

**I know the problem cold, but I don't know what to do Monday morning** — the deck is missing the action plan, the alternative sourcing options, the board resolution language, and any quantified scenario for our specific company. Give me the last 10 cards, or better yet, give me a single card with five numbered actions, owners, deadlines, and rupee costs.

# Strategic Intelligence Briefing — Visual Design Evaluation

## 1. TOP 3 CARDS (Best Visual-Message Alignment)

**Card 1 (c01) — Hero: "India faces the largest oil supply shock in history"**
The graduated horizontal bar chart comparing 1973 (~6%), 1979 (~9%), and current crisis (20%) is *perfectly* matched to the headline claim. The visual literally proves the "largest in history" assertion through proportional comparison. The pulsing animation on the current bar adds urgency without being gimmicky. The stat row reinforces without redundancy.

**Card 11 (c11) — "Losing fifty rupees on every litre of diesel"**
The waterfall chart is the *textbook correct* choice for showing cost build-up vs. a price ceiling. The annotation lines marking retail cap (₹87.57) and effective cost (₹140+) create an unmissable visual gap that IS the headline. You see the under-recovery without reading a word.

**Card 8 (c08) — "Jamnagar runs at full complexity. Single-source refineries are bleeding cash"**
The horizontal diverging bar chart with three red bars pointing left (OMC losses) and one green bar pointing right (RIL gain) is an instant visual proof of the headline's contrast. The zero-baseline annotation reinforces the divergence. This is a clean, correct chart selection.

---

## 2. BOTTOM 3 CARDS (Worst Visuals)

**Card 12 (c12) — "Russia waiver expires April 3"**
This is a **wall of text masquerading as a visual card**. The timeline uses `.tl-item` markup but renders as three paragraphs with dots. The progress bar at the bottom (67% filled) is the only actual data visualization for what is fundamentally a *countdown/Gantt problem*. Should be a **horizontal timeline bar** with clear phase segments (issued → today → expiry) sized proportionally to time, not a vertical text list. The three big numbers (30/10/0) are effective but arrive too late on the card.

**Card 9 (c09) — "Government overrode your product slate"**
The CSS "Sankey-style flow diagram" is ambitious but **fails as an information graphic**. The three horizontal bands don't communicate proportional flow — the LPG band says "MAX" (not a number), the widths don't encode data, and the left "100%" node connects to three outputs that don't sum to 100%. A proper **stacked bar or treemap** showing the before/after allocation split would prove the headline. What's here is decorative, not analytical.

**Card 10 (c10) — Act III Break: "Your Balance Sheet"**
While act breaks serve a narrative purpose, this card has **zero data visualization** for a section that names three quantifiable "clocks." The numbered list (01/02/03) with text descriptions is a missed opportunity for a **triple gauge or countdown timer visual** showing inventory days remaining, margin compression rate, and CAD widening. It reads like a PowerPoint agenda slide.

---

## 3. CHART AUDIT

| Card | Chart Type Used | Correct? | Verdict |
|------|----------------|----------|---------|
| c01 | Horizontal bars (proportional comparison) | ✅ **Yes** | Perfect for "biggest vs. historical" |
| c03 | Leaflet map with markers | ✅ **Yes** | Geographic data requires a map |
| c04 | Grouped bar (before/after by sector) | ✅ **Yes** | Before/after comparison across categories is textbook grouped bar |
| c05 | CSS timeline (horizontal axis with milestones) | ⚠️ **Marginal** | Works for milestone sequencing but labels overlap on mobile; a **Gantt bar** would better show duration of clearance phase |
| c08 | Horizontal bar (diverging) | ✅ **Yes** | Diverging bar around zero baseline is the correct choice for mixed positive/negative returns |
| c09 | CSS pseudo-Sankey | ❌ **Wrong** | Flows don't encode proportional data; use a **stacked 100% bar** or proper Sankey |
| c11 | Waterfall bar | ✅ **Yes** | Textbook waterfall for cost build-up |
| c12 | Vertical timeline + progress bar | ⚠️ **Underserved** | Should be a **horizontal Gantt/countdown bar** as the primary visual |
| c13 | Multi-line with scenario fork | ✅ **Yes** | Scenario divergence from a shared point is exactly right for a forking line chart |

---

## 4. TEXT-HEAVY CARDS

**Card 12 (c12)** — The waiver lifecycle is told in three dense paragraphs. This is the most text-heavy card with the clearest data-visualization alternative (a Gantt-style countdown).

**Card 7 (c07)** — MRPL shutdown. The capacity bar at the bottom is good, but the card is dominated by KPI boxes and text. The "100K of 300K" story would land harder as a **donut/gauge chart** (33% offline) as the hero visual, reducing surrounding text.

**Card 10 (c10)** — Act III break. Three numbered text blocks describing quantifiable phenomena (inventory drawdown, margin compression, CAD widening) that should each have a sparkline, gauge, or mini-chart attached.

**Card 6 (c06)** — Act II break. Entirely text. Acceptable for narrative pacing but contributes to a run of low-data-density cards.

---

## 5. VISUAL VARIETY — **7/10**

**Chart types observed:** horizontal bars (c01, c08), map (c03), grouped vertical bars (c04), CSS timeline (c05, c12), waterfall (c11), multi-series line (c13), CSS flow diagram (c09), KPI number panels (c02, c07), capacity bars (c07).

**Strengths:** Good mix of bar orientations, one map, one line chart, one waterfall. No two adjacent chart cards use the same type — the sequencing is well-considered.

**Weaknesses:** Heavy reliance on KPI-panel layouts (cards 2, 7, and elements within nearly every card). The "big number + colored border-left boxes" pattern repeats ~8 times across the deck. Two act-break cards (c06, c10) in 13 cards is generous pacing that dilutes data density. No small multiples, no slope charts, no scatter/bubble, no area charts — the palette could be wider.

---

## 6. ONE-LINE VERDICT

**Not quite FT/Bloomberg quality — it's 80% there.** The narrative architecture and typographic system are publication-grade, but three cards (c09's broken Sankey, c12's text-as-timeline, c10's chart-less act break) would be sent back in a newsroom review for stronger data-visual proof of their headlines.
